data.title: Kerberoasting - Service Accounts with Weak Passwords
data.summary:
Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for
accounts that have a registered Service Principal Name (SPN). The ticket is
encrypted using the service account's NTLM password hash, which allows the hash
to be extracted and subjected to offline brute-force attacks without generating
authentication failures or account lockouts.

Several service accounts within the domain were configured with weak,
human-generated passwords. These passwords were successfully recovered offline
within minutes using a standard wordlist.
data.description:
Any authenticated domain user is able to request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS)
for any account that has a Service Principal Name (SPN) registered against it.
This is standard Kerberos functionality and requires no elevated privileges; the
Key Distribution Centre performs no authorisation check to determine whether the
requesting user should have access to the service in question.

The returned ticket is encrypted using a key derived from the password of the
account the SPN belongs to. An attacker can therefore extract the encrypted
portion of the ticket and attempt to recover the account's plaintext password
offline, without any further interaction with the domain. Because the cracking
takes place entirely on attacker-controlled infrastructure, the activity produces
no failed authentication events, does not trigger account lockout, and is unlikely
to be detected by monitoring controls.

Service accounts within the domain were configured with passwords that did not
meet the length required to resist offline attack. Where a ticket is issued using
the legacy RC4 encryption type, cracking is substantially faster than against
AES-encrypted tickets. Several accounts returned tickets whose passwords were
recovered within minutes using a standard publicly available wordlist.

The exposure is increased where affected accounts hold privileges beyond those
required by the service they support, as recovery of the password grants the
attacker those privileges directly.
data.impact:
An attacker holding any valid domain account - including a low-privileged
account obtained through phishing or password spraying - could recover the
plaintext password of a privileged service account. Where such an account holds
elevated rights, this results in full compromise of the Active Directory domain,
granting access to all domain-joined systems, file shares, and the data they
contain.
data.recommendation:
1. Migrate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA). gMSA
   passwords are 120 characters, randomly generated, and rotated automatically
   by the domain controller.

2. Where gMSA is not supported by the application, configure the service account
   password to a minimum of 25 randomly generated characters and document a
   rotation schedule.

3. Remove Service Principal Names from accounts that do not require them.

4. Remove all service accounts from privileged groups such as Domain Admins,
   Enterprise Admins, and Account Operators. Grant only the specific rights the
   service requires.

5. Enable AES encryption for Kerberos on service accounts and disable RC4 where
   compatibility allows.
